summary:
Visitors in New Brunswick stand under Canada's national framework. Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code, both added by Bill C-16, which the Senate passed 67-11 in June 2017. Courts have applied those protections consistently, no jurisdiction restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities, legal gender recognition operates largely on self-declaration, and federally issued identity documents can carry an X marker. Entry carries no trans-specific friction.

Education is the layer where New Brunswick diverges from the national pattern. Policy 713 (Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity) of the Department of Education and Early Childhood Development has been in force since 17 August 2020, was revised on 1 July and 23 August 2023, and was revised again effective 1 January 2025. Under the current text a student of any age may choose the name and pronouns used for them in informal school settings, with parental consent encouraged but not required; only formal records for students under 16 still require parental consent. The revision restores the earlier position and goes further than the recommendations of child advocate Kelly Lamrock.

Policy 713's application clause covers the school environment as it involves all students together with school personnel, contract and casual employees, visiting professionals, student teachers, parents, volunteers, and visitors. Its name, pronoun and gender-neutral-facility provisions therefore apply to non-residents present in New Brunswick classrooms and school grounds, not only to enrolled pupils.

If a trans visitor is detained, the governing rules are federal rather than provincial. Correctional Service Canada's 2022 gender-diversity policy lets gender-diverse offenders request placement or transfer to a men's or women's institution matching their gender identity or expression, regardless of anatomy or the sex marker on identification documents; each request is assessed individually and may be refused where an unresolved overriding health or safety concern exists.
tangentialFactors:
The 2023 revision of Policy 713, effective 1 July 2023, barred teachers from using the preferred names and pronouns of students under 16 without parental consent and dropped explicit wording permitting students to take part in extracurricular activities, including sports teams, reflecting their gender identity. Premier Blaine Higgs's Progressive Conservative government made the change without a legislative vote, citing complaints from parents and teachers. Two ministers resigned in protest and two others were pushed out; eight Progressive Conservative members, six of them cabinet ministers, sat out question period on 9 June 2023 to object to the lack of process, and party dissidents called for a leadership review.

Public opposition was organised and sustained. About 350 people rallied at the New Brunswick legislature on 14 May 2023 against the review of the 2020 policy, which had required schools to respect students' chosen names and pronouns and to provide gender-neutral bathrooms. Gail Costello of Pride in Education, who helped write the policy, said it saved lives and warned that removing it would cost children. Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said trans kids in New Brunswick need to feel safe, not targeted by politicians.

Legal and administrative challenge accompanied the political fight. The Canadian Civil Liberties Association mounted a constitutional challenge to the 2023 consent rule, and the Holt government's revision effective 1 January 2025 undid that rule. New Brunswick's trajectory mirrors the wider pattern of sub-provincial policy turbulence in schools and sport seen elsewhere in Canada, where Saskatchewan's 2023 Education (Parents' Bill of Rights) Amendment Act and Alberta's 2024 education, health and sport statutes were shielded by notwithstanding-clause legislation.

National hate-crime data does not isolate trans incidents. Statistics Canada reported 4,882 police-reported hate-crime incidents in 2024, with incidents targeting sexual orientation down 26% to 658 from a 2023 peak of 889; the release breaks out sexual orientation rather than gender identity as a motivation category.
localsOnly:
For New Brunswick families, the practical position since 1 January 2025 is that a child of any age may use a chosen name and pronouns informally at school without parental permission, while changes to a student's formal record under the age of 16 still require a parent's signature. School personnel, contract and casual employees, visiting professionals, student teachers, parents, volunteers and visitors are all within the policy's scope, so the rules bind adults in the school environment as well as pupils.

Provincial correctional policy in New Brunswick is not specified in the available material. Provincial and territorial correctional rules vary across Canada, and no New Brunswick provincial-jail placement rule for trans detainees is documented. Trans people held in federal custody in the province fall under Correctional Service Canada instead.

Correctional Service Canada's placement data shows how the policy operates in practice. As of 2025 the agency recorded 90 self-identified transgender women in federal custody, 73 housed in men's institutions and 17 in women's. Between fiscal years 2017-18 and 2024-25 it received 129 placement or transfer requests from people assigned male at birth to women's institutions: 35 approved, 72 denied, 22 withdrawn.
outOfScopeNotes:
No New Brunswick provincial-jail placement rule for transgender detainees is documented in the available sources; that gap is unresolved rather than evidence that no rule exists.

The Correctional Investigator has criticised Correctional Service Canada's 2022 policy for unclear health-or-safety override criteria and for the absence of a dedicated abuse-reporting mechanism. A 2022 report alleged a pattern of abuse and discrimination against gender-diverse prisoners in Canadian jails, including greater exposure to sexual assault. How far these findings apply inside New Brunswick facilities is not sourced here.

Statistics Canada's hate-crime release does not break out gender identity as a motivation, so trans-specific hate-crime volume nationally and in New Brunswick is not established by that dataset.
